title: Short on Sleep, India Open New Zealand T20 Series on Two Days' Rest
excerpt: Shreyas Iyer's side flew in from a drawn West Indies series with barely two days to acclimatise before Thursday's Hagley Oval opener — and the captain says the churn is now built into the team's system.
body:
• India open the five-match T20I series against New Zealand at Hagley Oval, Christchurch, on Thursday, October 22, with barely two days to rest, acclimatise and train, according to PTI.
  • Captain Shreyas Iyer said the squad is used to the churn: "We are getting less sleep, but the more matches we play, the better it is for us."
  • Only four of India's batters — Iyer, Ishan Kishan, Sanju Samson and Shivam Dube — have previously played T20Is in New Zealand.
  • For US viewers, the opener starts at 12:30 PM IST on Thursday — 3:00 AM Eastern — with the series running to November 1 in Hamilton.

India's problem in Christchurch is not form. It is the clock. The Shreyas Iyer-led side has had barely two days to rest, acclimatise and train before Thursday's five-match T20I series opener against New Zealand at Hagley Oval, after a run that took them from the Asian Games in Japan to a home series against the West Indies that ended 2-2 on October 17. At his pre-match press conference, Iyer refused to use it as an excuse, according to the ICC's report.

"We have been playing so continuously, from Japan to India, from India to New Zealand. We are getting less sleep, but the more matches we play, the better it is for us."

— Shreyas Iyer, India T20I Captain

"We just want to put the reasons aside and see to it about how we would be planning to win," Iyer said. On conditions, he was equally direct: he has played in New Zealand before, the surfaces will not be completely different, and the job is to acclimatise as soon as possible and read each wicket on the day.

An inexperienced batting group in seaming conditions

The adaptation burden falls on a young batting order. PTI, in its series preview carried by Swadesi, noted that only four of India's chosen batters — Iyer, Ishan Kishan, Sanju Samson and Shivam Dube — have previously played T20Is in New Zealand. Abhishek Sharma, Tilak Varma and 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi are proven stroke-makers, but the nippy, seaming conditions will need adjustment. Iyer said Sooryavanshi, whose openers are scoring consistently, will use the trip to learn how to play on these wickets rather than walk straight into the side.

India's recent record here offers some comfort: unbeaten in their last two T20 series in New Zealand, their most recent clash on this soil, in Napier in 2022, ended in a rain-interrupted tie, with India claiming that series by winning the only match the weather allowed. The wider tour context — squads, the split captaincy and the ODI and Test legs that follow — is in our earlier tour preview.

Bowling is where Iyer wants the fix

By Iyer's own admission, reported by PTI, it is the bowling that needs fixing. India are without Jasprit Bumrah, who plays only the ODIs and Tests on this tour, and injured all-rounder Hardik Pandya. The return of Bhuvneshwar Kumar — back in the T20I setup for the first time since November 2022 — is the main corrective. "Bhuvi brings a lot of experience to the team," Iyer said. "In T20, if you see his career graph in the last two years, he has also won IPL, so he has a very good idea about how to dominate this format." Fit-again mystery spinner Varun Chakaravarthy adds a second experienced option, though questions remain over all-rounders Nitish Kumar Reddy and Shivam Dube, and India are unlikely to abandon their bat-to-number-eight model to strengthen the attack.

Iyer also framed the selection squeeze as a positive: competition motivates the current members to perform consistently, and every player has to be flexible about batting position because conditions and situations will demand it. He has batted at No. 3, No. 4 and No. 5 in recent months and said he is comfortable at any number.

Santner's counter: seam, and variety

New Zealand captain Mitchell Santner expects conditions to vary across the series and warned that offering flat tracks to a power-packed India may not be the best strategy. "If there is something in the pitch for the seamers to start, it's obviously nice, but throughout the series we're going around the country, they're not all going to be green seamers," Santner said. "Both teams are going to have to adapt quickly to the conditions." His pace options run deep — Jacob Duffy, Matt Henry, Adam Milne, Lockie Ferguson, Kyle Jamieson and Blair Tickner — while the injury-forced absence of Rachin Ravindra opens a route for Devon Conway to move up the order, with Glenn Phillips and Finn Allen supplying the power.

The stakes for Iyer extend beyond this week. His tenure began with back-to-back series losses in Ireland and England, and PTI noted he is expected to lead India at the T20 World Cup in Australia and New Zealand in two years' time. A series win here, on two days' rest, would be the strongest evidence yet that his side's adaptability is real. The first T20I starts at 12:30 PM IST on Thursday in Christchurch, followed by matches in Christchurch (October 24), Wellington (October 27), Auckland (October 30) and Hamilton (November 1).
